title: School-Based Intervention Programs: Conceptual, Empirical, Practical, and Equity-Focused Considerations Across Development, Implementation, Evaluation, and Dissemination
abstract: School-based intervention programs play an essential role in promoting students’ academic, behavioral, and social–emotional development. Achieving meaningful and equitable outcomes, however, depends on more than the availability of intervention programs. It also requires high-quality intervention work across the interconnected domains of intervention development, implementation, evaluation, and dissemination. Substantial scholarship exists within each domain, yet relevant concepts, considerations, and practical guidance are often distributed across separate studies and frameworks, making it difficult for intervention scientists and intervention adopters to develop an integrated understanding of intervention work. This paper provides a functional conceptualization of intervention work by synthesizing foundational concepts, empirical and practical considerations, and guiding questions across its four primary domains. Rather than proposing a new intervention framework, the paper complements existing frameworks by clarifying what each domain is intended to accomplish, the knowledge and products it generates, and how activities within one domain can inform and improve decisions made throughout the others. Collectively, the paper argues that high-quality intervention work depends not only on excellence within each domain, but also on intentionally designing activities within each domain so that the resulting knowledge and resources contribute to the broader system of intervention research and practice. The paper is written for two primary audiences: (a) intervention scientists engaged in developing, implementing, evaluating, or disseminating intervention programs, and (b) intervention adopters responsible for selecting, implementing, evaluating, and making continued-use decisions about programs in educational settings. Three primary contributions are provided. First, the paper clarifies foundational concepts, essential considerations, and key questions associated with each domain. Second, it illustrates how the four domains collectively contribute to the development, implementation, evaluation, dissemination, adoption, and sustained use of high-quality intervention programs. Third, it translates this conceptual perspective into practical guidance through tables, 12 key questions and considerations, and separate Reflection Guides designed to support professional judgment, high-quality intervention science, and evidence-driven intervention adoption and use.
